optionChallenges.claimRepresented: AS JSON with an nvarchar(max) column returns the complete nested detail object rather than a scalar field.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: This is supported, not incorrect. The path selects an existing object, the AS JSON flag requests a fragment, and nvarchar(max) satisfies that flag's required SQL type. Both items and memo remain within the returned object.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: For the supplied input, SELECT detail FROM OPENJSON(@payload) WITH (detail nvarchar(max) '$.detail' AS JSON); returns the detail fragment {"items":2,"memo":"ship"}. With N'{"detail":{"items":0,"memo":"hold"}}', the same projection preserves that different complete object.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: The type and AS JSON sections require nvarchar(max) for fragment projection and distinguish object/array extraction from scalar extraction. The order-object example returns a complete nested object alongside separately projected scalar fields.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: An nvarchar(max) output declaration alone makes ordinary OPENJSON projection return the selected object.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: Without AS JSON, this remains scalar extraction even though the SQL text type has maximum capacity. The selected detail is an object, so default lax mode returns NULL rather than its serialized fragment.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: For @payload = N'{"detail":"ready"}', SELECT detail FROM OPENJSON(@payload) WITH (detail nvarchar(max) '$.detail'); returns the scalar text ready. The option is unchanged; only a string-valued detail and a scalar-text requirement make it appropriate.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: AS JSON explicitly changes fragment-versus-scalar handling. Its absence selects scalar values, while selecting an object without the flag yields NULL in lax mode. The declared SQL text length does not replace that documented value-kind distinction.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: Projecting the items member as an integer preserves the entire detail object required for later processing.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: The exact path reaches only the number 2. Its SQL output type is int, not the required nvarchar(max), and memo is omitted. Keeping the alias detail does not retain the enclosing object's structure.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: On the original @payload, SELECT detail FROM OPENJSON(@payload) WITH (detail int '$.detail.items'); returns integer 2. This unchanged option is correct for a consumer needing only the typed item count, not the complete detail document.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: column_path identifies the value supplying a column, while type specifies its SQL result type. The typed-schema example separately extracts a nested quantity as INT and a whole order as AS JSON, demonstrating precisely this scalar-versus-fragment boundary.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: Returning the memo text as nvarchar(max) is equivalent to retaining the complete detail object.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: This selects the scalar ship, not the object containing both memo and items. Correct SQL text capacity and the output alias do not restore fields excluded by the narrower JSON path.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: Using the supplied @payload, SELECT detail FROM OPENJSON(@payload) WITH (detail nvarchar(max) '$.detail.memo'); returns ship. It is valid when the downstream contract requests only memo text. That changes the whole-object requirement, not the literal option.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: Explicit column paths override property selection, and projection without AS JSON extracts scalars. The article's mixed scalar/fragment example confirms that a nested scalar path returns that member rather than its enclosing object.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: OPENJSON (Transact-SQL): the independently read type and AS JSON sections require nvarchar(max) for object/array fragments and distinguish that operation from ordinary scalar projection. The mixed order example projects an entire object separately from typed nested fields. Default lax handling and the explicit return-schema contract establish NULL, integer 2 and memo text as the respective wrong outputs. Compatibility 160 satisfies the documented baseline.

choiceReviews.rationale: The path selects the existing detail object, and AS JSON requests its fragment rather than a scalar member. The declared nvarchar(max) also meets the flag's explicit type requirement. Thus the result retains both items and memo in one column. The unchanged definition likewise preserves {"items":0,"memo":"hold"} from N'{"detail":{"items":0,"memo":"hold"}}'. Neither a larger scalar type alone nor selecting a child field provides this documented fragment behavior.

The larger SQL text type does not change ordinary projection into fragment extraction. Because detail is an object and AS JSON is absent, default lax handling returns NULL instead of the object. The exact definition would correctly return ready from N'{"detail":"ready"}' when scalar text is required. That positive countercontext changes the property's JSON kind and the output contract, so it is not an alternative answer here.

This definition selects only $.detail.items and projects its value as integer 2. It cannot retain memo or the enclosing object, and its SQL output type also conflicts with the required nvarchar(max) column. On the same supplied document, the unchanged option is entirely valid for an item-count consumer. That narrower numeric requirement is a concrete correct countercontext, but it is explicitly not the complete-object task.

The path reaches the memo scalar ship and excludes items. Although its SQL output is nvarchar(max), that capacity does not recover the enclosing structure omitted by the path. Using the original document, the unchanged definition correctly serves a memo-only text consumer, returning ship under the alias detail. The candidate instead requires the whole object for later processing, so this otherwise valid scalar projection is insufficient.
